body:
> I wasn't party to the original proposal / implementation so have no idea why it was chosen to go that way. 

I asked for this design. It's a source separation. The idea is that the game speed is set by the game, and the "user" speed is set by the user in the editor.
Using the same variable for both is destructive: If the user overrides a game-specified value, it might unexpectedly speed up or slow down more or less than expected, because the base speed wasn't 1. If the game overrides a user-specified value, the user might be annoyed because their setting was disrespected. In a worse case (gradual change), the dropdown might not work at all.

Overall, using the same variable for both is good exactly when it's _supposed_ to be the same variable, for example if we recommend against using "game speed" for gameplay purposes (and only use it for debug). In that case, it would make more sense to share the variable. I can't comment on what share of users expect either behavior, but my default was "they're different features so they get different variables".

> I asked for this design. It's a source separation. The idea is that the game speed is set by the game, and the "user" speed is set by the user in the editor.

Sure, I'm not really referring to this. Different variables are needed when they need to be independent (this version does the same, with `wall_clock` scale and the old existing `game_time_scale`).

I'm more questioning whether iterations per second needs to be changing as far as the engine is concerned.

If we want to speed up and slow down the game while keeping everything the same, there's two ways to do it:

1) modify the ticks per second, and try and keep seconds "absolute"
2) count seconds slower or faster, keep everything else the same

We are now getting bug reports because of attempting to shoehorn in ticks per second which are not designed to be fractional.

So my question is more, rather than modifying tps, which can introduce a lot of subtle bugs, why didn't we simply change how time passes (as observed by the engine), which keeps such a change transparent to the rest of the engine (and users)?
Ah. I didn't review that part of the PR / feature (which is part of the reason why I never approved it).

To add further:

### Fixes Fragility
Modifying TPS at runtime is notoriously bug-prone in game engines. Fixed timesteps rely heavily on integer math or stable float deltas. Overriding ticks directly opens significant bug potential - subtle physics jitter, variable rounding errors and synchronisation bugs.

### Transparent Engine Execution
Scaling time via `get_ticks_usec()` means subsystems like animation, particle lifespans, physics steps don't have to alter their core math logic, they simply process what they believe to be standard delta time, unaware that the wall clock is ticking at a modified rate.

> So my question is more, rather than modifying tps, which can introduce a lot of subtle bugs, why didn't we simply change how time passes (as observed by the engine), which keeps such a change transparent to the rest of the engine (and users)?

The reason we don't *just* change the time scale is to ensure that when you use a different speed, it will behave more or less as if you ran it at normal speed. It basically aims to avoid the issue described in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/24334 (which can be worked around in scripts, but not in an editor-level toggle).

If your code doesn't consistently use delta time everywhere (which is common in complex enough projects), using the slow motion controls shouldn't introduce bugs due to that. As an analogy, it should behave like slow motion/turbo controls in emulators, which don't change the game's tickrate but change how often new frames are being simulated (while keeping the internal 60 Hz cadence).

If you have physics interpolation disabled, the game will look stuttery at low time scales (due to the decreased physics tick rate), but that's OK for development purposes.

See also `--fixed-fps`, which can cause a game to run faster or slower than intended while keeping its internal physics tick rate untouched.

> We are now getting bug reports because of attempting to shoehorn in ticks per second which are not designed to be fractional.

I think we could change `Engine.physics_ticks_per_second` to allow floating-point values, although this would break GDExtension compatibility unless we add a second property for it (and deprecate the integer-based one).

Thanks for the clarification. I think we are agreeing on the **goal** here, but the disagreement is purely on the **method** and the architectural layer where it is applied.

The emulator analogy is actually a good way to look at this, as there are two ways to achieve that exact behavior:

## Layer Separation
Modifying TPS at runtime is essentially like changing the virtual CPU hardware frequency inside an emulator. Because the underlying systems are designed around rigid, non-fractional cadences, shoehorning in fractional values introduces the precision and quantization bugs we are seeing in the issue tracker.

This PR takes the alternative approach: we leave the engine's internal tick rate and physics loop untouched. Instead, we scale `get_ticks_usec()` transparently. The engine still simulates its fixed cadence, but the wall clock it measures against moves slower or faster.

## Transparent Execution
This achieves 100% of the intent you described - it perfectly shields scripts that do not handle delta time correctly and maintains internal physics stability. However, it does so at the timing boundary rather than destabilizing core physics loops or forcing us to break GDExtension compatibility to support floating-point TPS values.

It is the identical end result for the developer, just implemented through a much less fragile mechanism.
